Unrequited means not returned or not given back in equal measure — especially when talking about feelings.

When you have a feeling toward someone, and that person does not feel the same way toward you in return, your feeling is unrequited.

That's the heart of it: one person feels something; the other person doesn't feel it back.
Understanding It More Deeply

Think of feelings like a bridge. For a bridge to connect two places, it needs to be built from both sides. If only one person is building it — laying bricks, pouring in effort and emotion — but the other person isn't building toward them at all, the bridge never meets in the middle. That is the picture "unrequited" paints.

The word almost always describes emotions — particularly deep or strong ones — that travel in only one direction.
The Most Common Use: Unrequited Love

By far, the most common phrase you will encounter is "unrequited love."

This means: Person A loves Person B deeply, but Person B does not love Person A back.

Sarah had been in love with her best friend for years, but he saw her only as a friend. Her love was unrequited.

Notice what's happening here:

  • Sarah's love is real and genuine — it's not weak or fake.
  • But it exists entirely on her side.
  • Her friend isn't returning that love.
  • So her love is unrequited — it goes out, but nothing comes back.

This situation is often painful, because the person doing the loving is emotionally vulnerable and invested, while the other person may not even be aware of it, or simply doesn't feel the same way.
A Crucial Nuance: It's Not the Same as "Rejected"

This is one of the most important distinctions to understand.

Rejected means someone was told "no" — they expressed their feelings, and the other person turned them down explicitly.

Unrequited is broader and softer. It simply means the feeling isn't returned. This can happen in several ways:

  • The other person may not know about the feeling at all (you never told them).
  • The other person may be aware but simply doesn't feel the same way.
  • The other person may have explicitly said no (which is also a form of unrequited feeling, but a more specific one).

So all rejected love is unrequited, but not all unrequited love involves a direct rejection. A person can quietly love someone from a distance for years — never saying a word — and that love is still unrequited, because it was never met with equal feeling from the other side.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

"Unrequited" is not a neutral, cold, clinical word. It carries a sense of longing, sadness, and emotional ache. It implies something tender and painful — the experience of caring deeply for someone who simply doesn't care back in the same way.

This is why the word appears so often in poetry, novels, songs, and films. It captures a very human kind of heartache: giving something precious — your love, your devotion — and receiving nothing in return.
Other Feelings That Can Be "Unrequited"

While love is the most common pairing, "unrequited" can describe other feelings too:

  • Unrequited affection — You feel warmth and fondness for someone who doesn't feel it back.
  • Unrequited admiration — You deeply admire someone who doesn't admire you in return (and may not even notice you).
  • Unrequited devotion — You are deeply loyal and dedicated to someone who doesn't reciprocate that loyalty.
  • Unrequited desire — You want someone who doesn't want you back.

The pattern is always the same: a feeling flows in one direction and is not met coming back the other way.
What "Unrequited" Does NOT Mean

• It does not mean the feeling is fake, silly, or less real. Unrequited love can be one of the most intense, genuine emotions a person feels.
  • It does not mean the other person is cruel or evil — they simply don't feel the same way, which is something no one can be forced to feel.
  • It does not automatically mean something dramatic happened. Sometimes unrequited love is quiet, private, and never spoken aloud.
The Register of the Word

"Unrequited" is a somewhat formal and literary word. You're more likely to read it in a book or hear it in a thoughtful conversation than in casual everyday chat. A teenager might say "I like him but he doesn't like me back" — but a writer or a more formal speaker would say "her feelings were unrequited."

This doesn't mean you can't use it in everyday life — you absolutely can — but it does give your language a slightly elegant, expressive quality when you use it.
A Few More Example Sentences

He spent his twenties chasing an unrequited passion for a woman who barely knew his name.

The poem is a beautiful meditation on unrequited love — the ache of loving someone who will never love you back.

Her unrequited admiration for her mentor quietly faded as the years passed.

There is nothing quite as isolating as unrequited devotion — giving everything to someone who gives you nothing in return.
Summary in One Sentence
Unrequited means a feeling — most often love — that is felt by one person but is not felt or returned by the other person, creating a painful emotional imbalance that flows in only one direction.
